gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 3000 W inverter on a 12 V battery draws at least 234 A (3000 W ÷ 12.8 V), while the usual 12 V 100 Ah LiFePO4 has a 100 A BMS and is rated for 1,280 W of output, so a 12 V 3000 W all-in-one on one such battery will be shut off by the battery's BMS long before it reaches its rated output. The maker's own 12 V 3000 W kit ships with two batteries and a 300 A DC breaker for this reason.
standout_why: I tried to open the Renogy pages ChatGPT got: the REGO 12V 3000W pages (results 4/5/7) and the 2000W HF page (result 9). renogy.com returned HTTP 429 on every try, so I could not check their text. I compared against what I could read: ChatGPT's answer and the result titles. The answer only says a 24 V or 48 V system 'reduces DC current' above about 2,000 W. It gives no amp figure, says nothing about the battery's BMS current limit, and does not say how many 12 V batteries a 3000 W unit needs. Results 1–3 and 12 are Renogy kit and RV pages, and their titles cover battery kWh, not the discharge current a 12 V inverter needs. I could not open them to confirm the body text.
decides: This doesn't change which inverter is the pick (ACOPOWER 3000W/12V is still the true all-in-one at $1,298). It decides whether the shopper's plan works. A 12 V 3000 W all-in-one needs a battery bank that can supply about 234 A or more: two or more 100 A-BMS 100 Ah batteries in parallel, or batteries with a higher-rated BMS, plus heavy cable and a roughly 300 A breaker. Sun Gold Power's own SGK-PRO3 kit is built exactly that way. On one Redodo 12V 100Ah (100 A BMS, 1,280 W), the shopper effectively has a 1,200–1,300 W inverter. If they need sustained loads near 3000 W, a 24 V unit halves the current.
